title: Planning the Physical Examination and Neurological Screening
lead: Examine with a purpose: every test must answer a question you formed in the history.

book.title: Planning the Physical Examination and Neurological Screening
book.lead: Examine with a purpose: every test must answer a question you formed in the history.

blocks.text: Before the patient undresses, stop for one minute and write your plan. This habit separates thoughtful clinicians from test collectors.

rows: What are my top three hypotheses?
Lumbar radiculopathy L5; hip-referred pain; piriformis-region pain
Cauda equina syndrome, fracture, vascular claudication
Moderate: one repetition of each movement, no overpressure
Do I need a neurological examination?
Yes: pain below the knee with tingling
Which special tests help my hypotheses?
Straight leg raise, slump, hip quadrant, FABER
What is my comparable sign (the test that reproduces the patient's problem)?
What will I measure to show change later?
Leg pain on flexion, SLR angle, Oswestry Disability Index

blocks.label: TEACHER'S VOICE
body: The "comparable sign" is your treasure. It is a test or movement that reproduces the patient's familiar symptom and can be measured. You will re-test it after each treatment to see if what you did helped.

items: **Observation**: posture, swelling, wasting, colour, scars, gait, how the patient moves and sits.
**Functional demonstration**: ask the patient to show the activity that hurts.
**Active movements**: range, quality, symptom response. Painful movements last.
**Passive movements**: compare with active. Feel the end-feel.
**Palpation**: after movement testing so that you do not irritate tissue early.
**Joint accessory movement** (passive intervertebral or peripheral joint glides).

rows: Active limited and painful, passive full and painful at the same point
Active and passive both limited in the same pattern
Active limited, passive full and pain-free
Weakness, neurological deficit or fear of movement
Movement limited by spasm with an empty end-feel (pain stops movement before tissue resistance)
Possible serious pathology or acute severe pain; be cautious
Patient stops you before any tissue resistance

blocks.text: Perform a neurological examination when the patient reports symptoms below the elbow or knee that suggest nerve involvement, numbness, tingling, weakness, or when you suspect spinal cord involvement.
Use a cotton wool tip. Touch one side then the matching point on the other side. Ask: "Does this feel the same on both sides?" Test the key areas, not the whole limb.

rows: Dorsum of foot, first web space

blocks.text: Hold each resisted position for about 3 to 5 seconds and compare sides. Fatiguing weakness on repetition can also be important.
Grade strength using the Medical Research Council (MRC) 0 to 5 scale: 0 no contraction, 1 flicker, 2 movement with gravity eliminated, 3 against gravity, 4 against some resistance, 5 normal.

rows: Thumb on the biceps tendon, tap your thumb
Arm supported, tap above the olecranon
Legs hanging free, tap the patellar tendon

blocks.text: Grade 0 absent, 1 reduced, 2 normal, 3 brisk, 4 with clonus. If a reflex seems absent, use reinforcement (Jendrassik manoeuvre: patient clenches teeth or pulls interlocked hands apart).

blocks.label: COMMON STUDENT TRAP
body: A reduced reflex on one side is meaningful. Symmetrically reduced reflexes are often normal for that person. Always compare sides and interpret with the whole picture.

blocks.text: Use this when you suspect spinal cord or brain involvement: symptoms in both arms or both legs, clumsy hands, gait disturbance, bladder change, or brisk reflexes.

rows: Flicking the middle finger's distal phalanx causes thumb and index finger flexion
Stroking the lateral sole causes big toe extension and toe fanning
More than a few rhythmic beats after quick dorsiflexion

sections.title: 3.5 Lower motor neuron versus upper motor neuron

rows: Lower motor neuron (nerve root, peripheral nerve)
Patterns of a limb, half body, or below a level

blocks.label: MEMORY HOOK
body: "Lower is less": lower motor neuron lesions give less tone, less reflex, less muscle bulk. Upper motor neuron lesions give more tone and more reflex.

items: **A patient has back pain only, no leg symptoms. Do you need full neurological testing?** Usually not routinely, but screen if the history suggests nerve involvement or red flags. Document why you did or did not.

**Biceps reflex reduced on the right, triceps brisk on both sides, Hoffmann positive. What do you think?** A mixed picture: a C5 to C6 root sign plus UMN signs suggests possible cervical myelopathy with root involvement. Stop manual therapy plans and arrange urgent medical review.
**Why do palpation after movement?** Early heavy palpation can irritate tissue and change later movement responses, making them harder to interpret.
**Active shoulder abduction is limited but passive is full. Name two causes.** Rotator cuff tear or weakness; C5 radiculopathy or axillary nerve palsy.

**What is an empty end-feel and why does it worry you?** The patient stops movement before any tissue resistance because of pain; it can indicate acute severe pathology, so proceed cautiously and screen for serious causes.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Write a one-minute examination plan from the history.
Perform a dermatome, myotome and reflex examination correctly.
Recognise lower and upper motor neuron patterns.
Identify and use a comparable sign.
